CausalChain: Chronic liver injury → activation of CAFs → secretion of CXCL11 → recruitment of T cell subsets that enhance tumor-initiating cell (stemness) properties → metabolic reprogramming in HCC elevates SAM/MTA → these metabolites induce epigenetic changes and upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules (PD-1/CTLA-4) → T cell exhaustion and impaired anti-tumor response.
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, simultaneous inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase (thereby reducing SAM/MTA driven T cell exhaustion) and blockade of the CXCL11/CXCR3 axis (thereby preventing pro-tumor T cell recruitment that supports cancer stem cell renewal) will synergistically restore effective anti-tumor immunity and reduce tumor progression.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents a challenging cancer due to its complex tumor microenvironment (TME), where chronic inflammation, immunosuppressive factors, and metabolic reprogramming converge to promote tumor progression and therapy resistance. Emerging evidence indicates that cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs) produce chemokines such as CXCL11 which not only recruit immune cells but, in certain contexts, support tumor‐initiating cell self‐renewal. Additionally, metabolic alterations in HCC cells elevate levels of immunosuppressive metabolites including S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA) that drive T cell exhaustion via upregulation of inhibitory receptors such as PD‐1 and CTLA‐4. Building on these intertwined mechanisms, combinatorial targeting of metabolic reprogramming and aberrant immune cell recruitment may unlock new therapeutic avenues for HCC.
